subtopics.title: Introduction to RAML
subtopics.meta_description: Learn RAML 1.0 fundamentals: resources, methods, data types, traits, resource types and includes for building design-first MuleSoft APIs from scratch.
subtopics.summary: A guided introduction to RAML 1.0 syntax and the reusable building blocks used to design REST APIs on Anypoint Platform.
subtopics.content_html:
Before you write a single line of Mule flow logic, a design-first API project starts with a specification. RAML (RESTful API Modeling Language) is a YAML-based language purpose-built for describing REST APIs, and it has historically been the specification format most tightly integrated with the Anypoint Platform, including API Designer, Exchange, Mocking Service, and APIkit.

Anatomy of a RAML Document

A RAML file always begins with a version header, followed by top-level metadata and then the resources that make up the API:

#%RAML 1.0
title: Customer API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}
mediaType: application/json

types:
  Customer:
    type: object
    properties:
      id: integer
      name: string
      email: string
      status:
        enum: [ACTIVE, INACTIVE]

/customers:
  get:
    description: Retrieve a list of customers
    responses:
      200:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: Customer[]
  post:
    description: Create a new customer
    body:
      application/json:
        type: Customer
    responses:
      201:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: Customer
  /{customerId}:
    get:
      responses:
        200:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: Customer
        404:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: string

Key RAML Building Blocks

  • Resources — URI paths such as /customers or nested /{customerId}, each supporting HTTP methods (get, post, put, delete, patch).
  • Types — reusable data shapes defined once under types and referenced throughout the API, similar in spirit to JSON Schema.
  • Traits — reusable partial method definitions (e.g. a "paged" trait adding offset/limit query parameters) applied to multiple methods with is: [paged].
  • Resource Types — reusable partial resource definitions that standardize common patterns like CRUD across many resources.
  • Examples — sample request/response bodies that power the Mocking Service and give consumers concrete usage references.
  • Includes — the !include tag lets you split large specifications into multiple files for maintainability.

Why Design-First With RAML

Designing the contract before writing implementation code lets API producers and consumers agree on the interface early, catch inconsistencies before development starts, and generate a working mock server for frontend or partner teams to integrate against immediately. Once the RAML is finalized, APIkit can scaffold an entire Mule application skeleton directly from it, guaranteeing that the implementation matches the published contract.

Tip: Publish your RAML fragments (data types, traits, security schemes) as reusable assets in Anypoint Exchange so multiple API projects across your organization share a single, consistent definition.

Traits and Resource Types in Practice

Traits shine when the same partial behavior repeats across many methods. A paged trait, for instance, can add standard offset and limit query parameters plus a documented 200 response shape, then be applied to every list-style GET endpoint with a single is: [paged] line rather than retyping the same parameters on every resource. Resource types work similarly but at the resource level, letting you define a generic collection pattern with GET and POST methods once, then reuse it for /customers, /orders, and /products alike, each parameterized with its own type. Together, traits and resource types keep large specifications DRY and consistent, which matters enormously once an API grows beyond a handful of endpoints and multiple designers are contributing to the same document.

Key Points

  • RAML 1.0 is a YAML-based specification language tightly integrated with Anypoint Platform tooling.
  • Resources, methods, types, traits, and resource types are the core reusable building blocks.
  • !include allows large specs to be split across multiple files.
  • Design-first RAML enables mocking, contract validation, and automatic scaffolding via APIkit.

subtopics.title: RAML Data Types In Depth
subtopics.meta_description: Explore RAML 1.0 data types in depth: scalars, objects, arrays, unions, enums and facets, plus how to define reusable types for consistent API contracts.
subtopics.summary: A detailed walkthrough of the RAML 1.0 type system, covering scalar and structured types, facets and reuse patterns.
subtopics.content_html:
RAML 1.0 introduced a full type system that goes well beyond the JSON Schema references RAML 0.8 relied on. Instead of bolting on an external schema language, RAML lets you describe every shape your API produces or consumes directly in the same file, using a syntax that reads like plain YAML. Getting comfortable with this type system is one of the highest-leverage skills for anyone doing design-first API work on Anypoint Platform, because well-modeled types drive validation, example generation, mocking and even the shape of generated APIkit flows.

Scalar Types

RAML ships with a set of built-in scalar types that map cleanly onto JSON and XML primitives: string, number, integer, boolean, date-only, time-only, datetime-only, datetime, file and nil. The datetime type additionally supports a format facet so you can pin it to rfc3339 or rfc2616 when your API needs a specific wire format rather than the RAML default.

Object Types

Object types are the workhorse of RAML modeling. You declare properties, mark individual properties as optional with a trailing ?, and RAML infers the rest as required. Objects can also declare additionalProperties: false to reject unexpected fields during validation.

#%RAML 1.0 Library
types:
  Address:
    type: object
    properties:
      street: string
      city: string
      postalCode:
        type: string
        pattern: "^[0-9]{5}$"
      country?: string

  Customer:
    type: object
    additionalProperties: false
    properties:
      id: integer
      name:
        type: string
        minLength: 1
        maxLength: 80
      age:
        type: integer
        minimum: 0
        maximum: 130
      status:
        enum: [ACTIVE, INACTIVE, SUSPENDED]
      tags?:
        type: array
        items: string
      billingAddress: Address
      shippingAddress?: Address

  CustomerOrId:
    type: Customer | integer

Array Types

Array types are declared either with the shorthand Customer[] or the longhand type: array plus an items facet, which is useful when you also need to constrain minItems, maxItems, or uniqueItems. Both notations are equivalent for simple cases, but the longhand form is required whenever you need to attach facets to the array itself rather than to its members.

Unions and Enums

The pipe operator (|) forms a union type, letting a property accept one of several shapes — useful for endpoints that return either a full resource or a lightweight reference. Enums restrict a scalar to a fixed set of literal values, which RAML tooling can turn directly into dropdowns or client-side constants.

Facets

Facets are the constraint keywords attached to a type to narrow the values it accepts. Strings support minLength, maxLength and pattern (a regular expression); numbers and integers support minimum, maximum, format and multipleOf; arrays support minItems, maxItems and uniqueItems. These facets are enforced automatically by APIkit's inbound validation, so a malformed payload is rejected with a 400 before your flow logic ever runs.

Reusing Types

Every type you define under the top-level types: section (or inside a RAML library) becomes referenceable by name anywhere else in the document, including inside other type definitions, as request/response bodies, and as query parameter types. This is what makes RAML modeling compositional: define Address once, then reuse it inside Customer, Order and Shipment without duplicating the field list.

CategoryExamplesTypical Facets
Scalarstring, number, integer, boolean, datetimepattern, minimum, maximum, format
ObjectCustomer, Address, Orderproperties, additionalProperties
ArrayCustomer[], array of stringminItems, maxItems, uniqueItems
UnionCustomer | integer(inherits facets of each member)

Key Points

  • RAML's built-in scalars cover the same ground as JSON primitives plus dedicated date/time variants.
  • Object types use properties, optional ? suffixes, and additionalProperties: false for strict validation.
  • Arrays can be declared with the Type[] shorthand or the longhand form when facets like minItems are needed.
  • Union types (|) and enums model "one of several" values without external schemas.
  • Facets such as pattern, minLength and minimum/maximum give you declarative validation enforced automatically by APIkit.
  • Defining types once under types: and referencing them everywhere keeps large specs consistent and DRY.

subtopics.title: RAML Traits
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how RAML traits let you reuse method-level behavior like pagination, auth headers and rate limiting across resources, including parameterized traits.
subtopics.summary: An explanation of RAML traits, the reusable method-level building blocks used to avoid repeating common request and response behavior.
subtopics.content_html:
Real APIs tend to repeat the same handful of behaviors across dozens of endpoints: pagination query parameters, rate-limit response headers, standard error responses on a secured method. Copy-pasting these details into every method definition is exactly the kind of duplication RAML was designed to eliminate, and the mechanism it provides for method-level reuse is called a trait.

What a Trait Is

A trait is a partial method definition — a fragment containing any of the things a method can declare, such as queryParameters, headers, responses or a description. Traits do not stand alone; they are mixed into a concrete get, post, put, delete or patch definition using the is: keyword, either at the method level or at the resource level (where it applies to every method on that resource).

#%RAML 1.0
title: Catalog API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}

traits:
  secured:
    description: Requires a valid bearer token
    headers:
      Authorization:
        description: Bearer token
        type: string
    responses:
      401:
        body:
          application/json:
            example: |
              { "error": "Unauthorized" }

  paginated:
    queryParameters:
      offset:
        type: integer
        default: 0
        minimum: 0
      limit:
        type: integer
        default: 20
        maximum: 100

  rateLimited:
    description: Limited to <<maxCalls>> calls per <<period>>
    responses:
      429:
        description: Too many requests, limited to <<maxCalls>> per <<period>>

/products:
  get:
    is: [ secured, paginated, rateLimited: { maxCalls: 100, period: "minute" } ]
    responses:
      200:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: Product[]

Parameterized Traits

Traits become dramatically more useful once you parameterize them. Any token written as <<tokenName>> inside a trait is a placeholder that gets substituted when the trait is applied. In the rateLimited trait above, <<maxCalls>> and <<period>> are filled in at the point of use, so the same trait definition can describe a 100-per-minute limit on one endpoint and a 10-per-second limit on another without duplicating the trait itself.

Applying Multiple Traits

The is: array can list any number of traits, and RAML merges their contents into the method definition. Order in the list does not imply precedence for most fields, but when two traits declare the same response code, tooling behavior can vary, so it is best practice to keep traits focused on non-overlapping concerns (one trait for auth, one for paging, one for rate limiting) rather than building a single monolithic trait.

Resource-Level Application

Traits are not limited to individual methods. Declaring is: [secured] directly on a resource applies that trait to every method nested underneath it, which is a convenient shortcut for resources where every operation requires the same header or response.

Traits vs. Resource Types

Traits and resource types both exist to eliminate duplication, but they operate at different levels of granularity. A trait augments an existing method with extra headers, parameters or responses; it never defines a method on its own. A resource type, by contrast, can define whole methods from scratch, including bodies. In practice, a well-organized RAML spec uses resource types to establish the overall shape of an endpoint (list, create, retrieve) and layers traits on top for cross-cutting concerns like authentication or pagination that apply across many otherwise-different resources.

TraitTypical PurposeCommon Parameters
securedAdds an Authorization header and 401 responsenone, or a scheme name
paginatedAdds offset/limit query parametersdefaultLimit, maxLimit
rateLimitedDocuments throttling behavior and a 429 responsemaxCalls, period

Key Points

  • A trait is a reusable, partial method definition mixed in with the is: keyword.
  • Traits can be applied to a single method or to an entire resource, cascading to all its methods.
  • Parameterized traits use <<tokenName>> placeholders that are filled in at each application site.
  • Keeping each trait focused on one concern (auth, paging, rate limiting) avoids conflicting merges.
  • Traits reduce duplication without generating extra resources, unlike resource types which model whole endpoints.

subtopics.title: RAML Resource Types
subtopics.meta_description: Understand RAML resource types for reusing entire endpoint patterns such as CRUD collections and members, with fully parameterized, real-world examples.
subtopics.summary: A practical guide to RAML resource types, the mechanism for reusing full resource-level patterns like collection and member endpoints.
subtopics.content_html:
Where traits reuse a slice of a method's behavior, resource types reuse an entire resource's shape — the full set of methods, their bodies and their responses. If your API has ten resources that all follow the same "list, create, retrieve, update, delete" CRUD pattern, a resource type lets you write that pattern once and apply it ten times, dramatically shrinking the spec and keeping every resource consistent.

Defining a Resource Type

A resource type is declared under the top-level resourceTypes: section. Inside it you write method stubs (get, post, and so on) exactly as you would on a real resource, including bodies, responses and query parameters. Two special shorthand names, get and post, can appear without a colon-body when you only need to mark the method as present without extra detail, but most real resource types spell out full bodies and responses.

#%RAML 1.0
title: Inventory API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}

types:
  Product:
    type: object
    properties:
      id: integer
      name: string
      price: number

resourceTypes:
  collection:
    get:
      description: List all <<resourcePathName>>
      responses:
        200:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: <<typeName>>[]
    post:
      description: Create a new <<resourcePathName|!singularize>>
      body:
        application/json:
          type: <<typeName>>
      responses:
        201:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: <<typeName>>

  member:
    get:
      description: Retrieve a single <<resourcePathName|!singularize>>
      responses:
        200:
          body:
            application/json:
              type: <<typeName>>
        404:
          description: Not found
    delete:
      description: Remove a <<resourcePathName|!singularize>>
      responses:
        204:

/products:
  type: { collection: { typeName: Product } }
  /{productId}:
    type: { member: { typeName: Product } }

Parameters and Built-in Transformers

Like traits, resource types support <<tokenName>> parameters, but they also get two automatic tokens for free: <<resourcePathName>> (the last segment of the resource's URI) and <<resourcePath>> (the full path). RAML also ships built-in string transformers you can pipe a token through, such as !singularize, !pluralize, !uppercase and !lowercamelcase, which is how the example above turns products into "product" for singular descriptions.

Resource Types vs. Traits

It is easy to conflate the two, so it helps to think of resource types as answering "what does this whole endpoint look like" and traits as answering "what extra behavior does this one method need." They compose together: a resource can have both a type and an is list at the same time.

Overriding Inherited Behavior

A resource that applies a type is free to add its own methods or override individual facets of an inherited method — declaring a description or additional responses directly on the resource layers on top of, rather than replaces, what the resource type contributed. This lets you keep a shared pattern for the common case while still accommodating the occasional resource that needs an extra response code or a stricter body type.

AspectResource TypeTrait
ScopeWhole resource (multiple methods)Single method (or all methods on a resource)
Keywordtype:is:
Typical useCRUD patterns, collection/member shapesPagination, auth headers, rate limits
Can combine with the other?YesYes

Key Points

  • Resource types reuse an entire resource's method set, bodies and responses, declared under resourceTypes:.
  • Apply one with type: typeName or type: { typeName: { param: value } } for parameterized versions.
  • Built-in tokens like <<resourcePathName>> plus transformers like !singularize reduce boilerplate further.
  • Resource types and traits solve different problems and are commonly combined on the same resource.
  • Standardizing CRUD resources this way keeps large APIs consistent as they grow.

subtopics.title: RAML Security Schemes
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how to define OAuth 2.0, Basic Authentication and API Key security schemes in RAML 1.0, then apply them to resources and methods with securedBy.
subtopics.summary: A walkthrough of declaring reusable security schemes in RAML and applying them across an API with the securedBy keyword.
subtopics.content_html:
Documenting an API's authentication requirements as prose comments is easy to get wrong and easy for consumers to miss. RAML instead treats security as a first-class, structured concept: you declare named security schemes once, describing exactly what headers, query parameters or OAuth flows they require, and then attach those schemes to resources or methods with a single keyword.

The securitySchemes Section

Security schemes live under a top-level securitySchemes: section. Each scheme has a type — commonly OAuth 2.0, Basic Authentication, Digest Authentication, Pass Through (the closest fit for a simple API key) or x-custom for anything else — plus a describedBy block that documents the exact headers, query parameters and responses associated with using that scheme.

#%RAML 1.0
title: Payments API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}

securitySchemes:
  oauth2:
    type: OAuth 2.0
    describedBy:
      headers:
        Authorization:
          description: Bearer access token
          type: string
      responses:
        401:
          description: Missing or invalid token
        403:
          description: Insufficient scope
    settings:
      authorizationUri: https://auth.example.com/oauth2/authorize
      accessTokenUri: https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token
      authorizationGrants: [authorization_code, client_credentials]
      scopes: ["payments:read", "payments:write"]

  apiKey:
    type: Pass Through
    describedBy:
      headers:
        X-Api-Key:
          description: API key issued in the developer portal
          type: string
      responses:
        401:
          description: Missing or invalid API key

  basicAuth:
    type: Basic Authentication
    describedBy:
      responses:
        401:
          description: Invalid username or password

securedBy: [apiKey]

/payments:
  post:
    securedBy: [oauth2]
    body:
      application/json:
        type: object
    responses:
      201:

Applying Schemes with securedBy

The securedBy: keyword accepts a list, and it can appear at the root of the document (applying a default to every resource), on a specific resource, or on an individual method, with the more specific declaration overriding the root default. Passing null as one of the list entries marks that scope as explicitly unsecured, which is useful for a public health-check endpoint on an otherwise secured API.

OAuth 2.0 Settings

For the OAuth 2.0 type, the settings block captures the details RAML understands natively: authorizationUri, accessTokenUri, the allowed authorizationGrants (authorization_code, client_credentials, password, implicit), and a scopes list. Anypoint API Manager and Design Center can read these settings to pre-populate policy configuration and interactive documentation.

Choosing a Scheme Type

RAML does not have a dedicated "API Key" type; the community convention is to model a header- or query-parameter-based key using Pass Through, since that type exists specifically for schemes RAML does not need to validate the mechanics of, only document.

Security Schemes and API Manager Policies

Declaring a security scheme in RAML is purely descriptive — it documents the contract but does not enforce anything at runtime by itself. Actual enforcement in a deployed Mule application comes from an API Manager policy (such as an OAuth 2.0 Access Token Enforcement policy, a Basic Authentication policy, or a Client ID Enforcement policy) applied to the proxy or the API implementation. Keeping the RAML securitySchemes block aligned with the policies actually configured in API Manager avoids a common source of confusion where the published contract promises one authentication mechanism while the runtime enforces another.

Scheme TypeTypical UseKey Settings
OAuth 2.0Delegated auth with scopesauthorizationUri, accessTokenUri, scopes
Basic AuthenticationUsername/password over HTTPS(none required)
Pass ThroughAPI keys, custom headersdescribedBy headers/queryParameters
x-customAnything not otherwise modeledFully custom describedBy

Key Points

  • Security schemes are declared once under securitySchemes: and reused via securedBy:.
  • securedBy can be set at root, resource, or method level, with more specific scopes overriding broader ones.
  • OAuth 2.0 schemes carry a settings block with authorization/token URIs, grants and scopes.
  • API keys are typically modeled with the Pass Through type plus a header or query parameter in describedBy.
  • Using null in a securedBy list explicitly marks an endpoint as unsecured.

subtopics.title: RAML Libraries, Includes and Overlays
subtopics.meta_description: See how RAML's !include directive, uses libraries, overlays and extensions let large API specs be split across files and adapted for different variants.
subtopics.summary: An overview of the file-organization tools RAML provides, from raw includes to full libraries, overlays and extensions.
subtopics.content_html:
A single RAML file describing a large API quickly becomes unwieldy: hundreds of lines of types, dozens of resources, and multiple security schemes all in one document. RAML provides three complementary mechanisms for splitting specifications across files and adapting a base spec for different needs: the raw !include tag, structured libraries, and overlays/extensions.

The !include Directive

The simplest tool is !include, a YAML custom tag that pulls the contents of another file in verbatim at that point in the document. It works for whole fragments (a types file, an examples file, even a whole resource) and is commonly used to keep example payloads out of the main spec file.

#%RAML 1.0
title: Orders API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}

types:
  Order: !include types/order.raml

/orders:
  post:
    body:
      application/json:
        type: Order
        example: !include examples/order-example.json
    responses:
      201:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: Order

Libraries with uses:

A RAML library is a dedicated file (conventionally starting with #%RAML 1.0 Library) that bundles related types, traits, resource types and security schemes for reuse across multiple API specs, not just multiple resources within one spec. A library is imported with the uses: keyword, bound to a namespace, and its contents are then referenced with a dotted prefix.

#%RAML 1.0 Library
usage: Common types shared across the Commerce APIs
types:
  Money:
    type: object
    properties:
      amount: number
      currency: string

traits:
  paginated:
    queryParameters:
      offset: integer
      limit: integer
#%RAML 1.0
title: Orders API
version: v1
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}
uses:
  common: libraries/common.raml

types:
  Order:
    type: object
    properties:
      id: integer
      total: common.Money

/orders:
  get:
    is: [ common.paginated ]
    responses:
      200:

Overlays and Extensions

Overlays and extensions both start from an existing, complete RAML document and layer changes on top of it without editing the original file. An overlay is restricted to non-structural changes — documentation, descriptions, examples, annotations — and cannot add or remove resources, methods or types. An extension is more powerful and can add new resources, methods, security schemes or types, making it suitable for describing an environment-specific or partner-specific variant of a base API. Both use extends: pointing at the master file and only need to include the fragments that differ.

#%RAML 1.0 Overlay
extends: orders-api.raml
title: Orders API (Spanish Documentation)
/orders:
  get:
    description: Recupera una lista de pedidos

Choosing the Right Tool

Use !include for simple file splitting within one spec, a library when the same types/traits/schemes need to be shared across several independent API specs, an overlay for purely descriptive variants (translations, extra documentation), and an extension when a partner or environment genuinely needs extra resources or fields on top of the base contract.

MechanismCan Add Structure?Typical Use
!includeN/A (raw file inclusion)Splitting one spec into multiple files
Library (uses:)N/A (defines reusable building blocks)Sharing types/traits across many APIs
OverlayNoTranslations, extra docs, examples
ExtensionYesPartner- or environment-specific variants

Key Points

  • !include pulls another file's raw contents in at a given point, ideal for keeping large specs manageable.
  • RAML libraries bundle types, traits, resource types and security schemes for reuse across multiple API projects via uses:.
  • Overlays add documentation-only changes on top of a base spec; they cannot alter structure.
  • Extensions can add new resources, methods or types on top of a base spec for environment- or partner-specific variants.
  • Both overlays and extensions reference the base file with extends: and only need to declare what changes.

subtopics.title: RAML Examples and Annotations
subtopics.meta_description: Understand how RAML's example and examples keywords power mocking and Design Center tooling, and how custom annotations extend a spec with extra metadata.
subtopics.summary: A closer look at how sample payloads and custom annotations make a RAML specification more useful for tooling and API consumers.
subtopics.content_html:
A type definition tells consumers the shape of a payload, but it does not tell them what a realistic payload actually looks like. RAML closes that gap with the example and examples keywords, and it lets teams attach arbitrary structured metadata to any part of a spec through annotations. Both features matter more than they might first appear, because Anypoint's Mocking Service, API Console and Design Center all read directly from them.

Single Examples

The singular example keyword attaches one sample value to a type or a body. It can be inline, or pulled from a file with !include, which keeps large JSON or XML samples out of the main spec.

types:
  Product:
    type: object
    properties:
      id: integer
      name: string
      price: number
    example:
      id: 1024
      name: Wireless Mouse
      price: 24.99

/products/{productId}:
  get:
    responses:
      200:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: Product
            example: !include examples/product-example.json

Multiple Named Examples

When one payload shape needs several representative variations — a minimal order versus a fully discounted order, for instance — the plural examples keyword accepts a map of named samples instead of a single value. Anypoint's Mocking Service can then be asked to return a specific named example by request header, which is invaluable for testing edge cases against a mock before any backend exists.

    responses:
      200:
        body:
          application/json:
            type: Order
            examples:
              minimal:
                id: 1
                items: []
                total: 0
              discounted:
                id: 2
                items: [ { sku: "ABC", qty: 3 } ]
                total: 45.00
                discountCode: "SUMMER10"

Why Examples Matter

RAML can auto-generate an example from a type definition if none is supplied, but a hand-written example communicates intent that a schema alone cannot: realistic identifiers, believable string lengths, sensible enum choices. This is what makes the Mocking Service and Design Center's "Try It" console produce responses that look like real data rather than string or 0 placeholders, and it gives frontend teams something concrete to build against before the backend flow exists.

Custom Annotations

Annotations let you attach arbitrary, structured metadata anywhere in a RAML document — on a resource, a method, a type, even a property — using parenthesized syntax: (annotationName). Before an annotation can be used it must be declared under annotationTypes:, which defines the shape the metadata must take, exactly like defining a regular type.

annotationTypes:
  deprecated:
    type: object
    properties:
      since: string
      replacement: string
  audience:
    type: string
    enum: [internal, partner, public]

/legacy-orders:
  (deprecated):
    since: "v2"
    replacement: "/orders"
  (audience): internal
  get:
    description: Deprecated in favor of /orders
    responses:
      200:

Common uses include marking deprecated endpoints, tagging resources for internal governance dashboards, recording the owning team, or feeding custom code-generation templates with information RAML's built-in vocabulary has no keyword for.

FeatureKeywordPrimary Consumer
Single sample payloadexampleAPI Console, Mocking Service
Multiple named samplesexamplesMocking Service (select by header)
Custom metadata(annotationName) + annotationTypesGovernance tooling, code generators

Key Points

  • example attaches one sample payload; examples attaches several named variants.
  • Examples can be inlined or pulled from external files with !include to keep specs readable.
  • Hand-written examples produce far more realistic mock responses than auto-generated ones.
  • Annotations use (name) syntax and must first be declared under annotationTypes:.
  • Annotations are a clean extension point for metadata RAML has no built-in keyword for, such as deprecation notices or ownership tags.

subtopics.title: APIkit Router
subtopics.meta_description: See how the APIkit Router maps incoming HTTP requests to Mule flows using naming conventions, and how it generates built-in 404, 405 and 400 error flows.
subtopics.summary: How the APIkit Router dispatches requests to flows by naming convention and auto-generates standard error-handling flows.
subtopics.content_html:
Once an API contract exists as RAML or OAS, APIkit is the Mule module that turns it into a running implementation. Its central component, the APIkit Router, inspects each incoming HTTP request, matches it against the specification, and dispatches it to the correct flow — without you having to hand-write routing logic for every resource and method.

How the Router Matches Requests

The router is configured with a reference to an apikit:config element that points at your RAML or OAS file. Based on the specification, APIkit expects flows to be named using a strict convention: <http-method>:\<resource-path>:<config-name>. When a request arrives, the router parses the method and path, finds the matching resource in the spec, and invokes the correspondingly named flow.

<apikit:config name="customer-api-config"
    api="customer-api.raml"
    outboundHeadersMapName="outboundHeaders"
    httpStatusVarName="httpStatus" />

<flow name="customer-api-main">
    <http:listener path="/api/*" config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" />
    <apikit:router config-ref="customer-api-config" />
    <error-handler ref="global-error-handler" />
</flow>

<flow name="get:\customers:customer-api-config">
    <flow-ref name="list-customers-subflow" />
</flow>

<flow name="get:\customers\(customerId):customer-api-config">
    <flow-ref name="get-customer-by-id-subflow" />
</flow>

<flow name="post:\customers:customer-api-config">
    <flow-ref name="create-customer-subflow" />
</flow>

Built-In Error Flows

APIkit automatically generates a small set of error-handling flows that fire when a request doesn't match the contract:

  • api-kit:notFound — fires when the requested path doesn't exist in the specification, producing a 404.
  • api-kit:methodNotAllowed — fires when the path exists but the HTTP method isn't defined for it, producing a 405.
  • api-kit:notAcceptable / unsupportedMediaType — fire on content negotiation and body media type mismatches.
  • api-kit:badRequest — fires when the request body fails schema validation against the spec.

These correspond to APIKIT:* error types that can be caught in an error handler just like connector errors, letting you normalize their response bodies alongside your own business errors.

<on-error-propagate type="APIKIT:BAD_REQUEST">
    <set-payload value='{"error": "Bad Request", "message": error.description}' />
    <set-variable variableName="httpStatus" value="400" />
</on-error-propagate>

The Main Flow Pattern

Best practice keeps the flow containing apikit:router extremely thin — just the listener, the router, and an error handler reference — while every generated resource/method flow immediately delegates to a descriptively named subflow that contains the actual business logic. This separation keeps the auto-generated routing layer untouched by developers and makes the implementation easy to navigate.

Note: If you regenerate flows from an updated specification, APIkit will not overwrite subflows you created yourself, only the routing flows it manages — provided you followed the recommended pattern of delegating out of the generated flows immediately.

Content Negotiation and Payload Validation

Beyond routing, the router also enforces the contract's data expectations. If a request specifies an Accept header that the resource's spec cannot satisfy, or submits a body in a media type the operation doesn't declare, the router short-circuits straight to the corresponding error flow instead of invoking your business logic at all. When request body schemas are defined in the RAML or OAS document, APIkit can validate incoming payloads against them automatically, rejecting malformed requests with a 400 before they ever reach your flow. This keeps validation logic out of your business flows entirely: the contract itself becomes the single source of truth for what a valid request looks like, and your handwritten logic only has to deal with requests it can trust.

Key Points

  • APIkit Router matches incoming requests to flows using a strict method:\resource:config naming convention.
  • It auto-generates 404, 405, 406/415, and 400 error flows tied to APIKIT:* error types.
  • Keep router flows thin and delegate immediately to subflows for maintainability.
  • The router works against both RAML and OpenAPI specifications.

subtopics.title: Designing APIs with API Designer
subtopics.meta_description: Explore Anypoint Design Center's API Designer: the RAML/OAS editor, live Mocking Service, reusable fragments, and the full design-first API workflow it enables.
subtopics.summary: A walkthrough of the design-first workflow in Anypoint Design Center, from drafting a spec to publishing it to Exchange.
subtopics.content_html:
Anypoint Design Center's API Designer is where design-first API development happens visually and collaboratively, before any Mule implementation exists. It gives architects and API designers a browser-based editor purpose-built for RAML and OpenAPI, with live validation and an instantly runnable mock.

What API Designer Provides

  • Syntax-aware editor — autocompletion, inline validation, and structure navigation for RAML and OAS documents, catching malformed specs before they reach implementation.
  • Visual editor — a form-based view for building resources, methods, types, and responses without hand-writing YAML, useful for teams that are less comfortable with raw specification syntax.
  • Console / documentation preview — a live, interactive rendering of the API so reviewers can browse resources and try sample requests.
  • Mocking Service — automatically spins up a mock endpoint that returns realistic example responses defined in the spec, letting consumer teams start integration work before the real implementation exists.
  • Fragments — reusable RAML pieces (data types, traits, security schemes, resource types) that can be saved to Exchange and referenced from multiple API projects.

A Typical Design-First Workflow

  1. An architect creates a new API project in Design Center and chooses RAML or OpenAPI as the specification format.
  2. Resources, methods, request/response schemas, and example payloads are defined, often reusing type and trait fragments pulled in from Exchange.
  3. The Mocking Service is enabled, giving stakeholders and frontend developers a working sandbox to test against immediately.
  4. The specification is reviewed, iterated on with business and consumer teams, and versioned.
  5. Once approved, the API is published to Anypoint Exchange as an asset with a defined group, name, and version.
  6. A developer imports the published asset into Anypoint Studio and uses APIkit to scaffold the Mule implementation directly from the contract.

Security Schemes

API Designer also lets you declare reusable security schemes — for example an OAuth 2.0 or Basic Authentication scheme — once, and apply them to individual methods or the entire API:

securitySchemes:
  oauth_2_0:
    type: OAuth 2.0
    describedBy:
      headers:
        Authorization:
          type: string
    settings:
      authorizationUri: https://login.example.com/authorize
      accessTokenUri: https://login.example.com/token
      authorizationGrants: [authorization_code]

/customers:
  get:
    securedBy: [oauth_2_0]

Why Design in Exchange-Connected Design Center Rather Than Locally

Designing directly in Design Center, instead of writing RAML in a local text editor, keeps the specification tied to Anypoint Exchange from day one: version history, dependency management for fragments, and governance rules (API design standards enforced through Anypoint Governance) apply automatically. It also makes hand-off to implementation teams frictionless, since the published asset is immediately importable into Studio as the source for APIkit scaffolding.

Tip: Treat your RAML/OAS fragments as shared libraries. A single "Common Types" fragment for error responses and pagination keeps every API in your organization consistent and dramatically reduces duplicated specification code.

Key Points

  • API Designer is Anypoint Design Center's browser-based tool for authoring RAML/OAS specifications.
  • The Mocking Service lets consumers integrate before implementation is built.
  • Fragments and security schemes promote reuse across multiple API projects.
  • Publishing to Exchange bridges the design-first workflow into APIkit-based implementation in Studio.

subtopics.title: OpenAPI Specification (OAS)
subtopics.meta_description: Understand OpenAPI (OAS) document structure, paths and components, and how it compares to RAML for design-first API development using APIkit in Mule 4.
subtopics.summary: How OpenAPI documents are structured and how OAS compares to RAML for API design and APIkit implementation.
subtopics.content_html:
While RAML has deep roots in the Anypoint ecosystem, the OpenAPI Specification (OAS) is the industry-standard, most widely adopted way to describe REST APIs across the broader software world. MuleSoft has invested heavily in first-class OAS support, and modern Anypoint Platform tooling — Design Center, Exchange, API Manager, and APIkit — treats OAS as a peer to RAML.

Structure of an OAS Document

OpenAPI documents can be written in YAML or JSON. A typical OAS 3.0 document is organized around info, paths, and reusable components:

openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: Customer API
  version: "1.0.0"
  description: API for managing customer records
servers:
  - url: https://api.example.com/v1
paths:
  /customers:
    get:
      summary: List customers
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A list of customers
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/Customer'
    post:
      summary: Create a customer
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/Customer'
      responses:
        '201':
          description: Customer created
components:
  schemas:
    Customer:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
        name:
          type: string
        email:
          type: string
      required: [name, email]

RAML vs OpenAPI

AspectRAML 1.0OpenAPI (OAS)
FormatYAML onlyYAML or JSON
EcosystemStrong within Anypoint PlatformBroad industry adoption, huge tool ecosystem
Reuse mechanismTraits, resource types, !includeComponents with $ref
APIkit supportFull supportFull support (APIkit for OAS)
Typical originMuleSoft-centric teamsCross-platform / polyglot organizations

Using OAS With APIkit

APIkit for OAS works the same way as it does for RAML: point apikit:config at an OAS file, and the router matches requests to flows using the same method:\resource:config naming convention, generating equivalent 404/405/400 error flows tied to APIKIT:* error types.

<apikit:config name="customer-api-config"
    api="customer-api-oas.yaml"
    outboundHeadersMapName="outboundHeaders"
    httpStatusVarName="httpStatus" />

Choosing Between Them

If your organization already standardizes on OpenAPI for non-Mule services, or you need to integrate with tools expecting OAS (API gateways, code generators, third-party documentation platforms), OAS is usually the pragmatic choice. If your team is deeply invested in Anypoint-native patterns like RAML traits and resource types, RAML remains fully supported and equally capable for Mule-based implementations.

Note: Anypoint Exchange and API Manager both support publishing, versioning, and applying policies to APIs regardless of whether they are described in RAML or OAS.

Importing Existing OAS Documents

A common real-world scenario is inheriting an OpenAPI document that already exists — perhaps written by a partner team, generated from a Spring Boot or Node.js service, or exported from another API gateway. Anypoint Platform can import these directly into Design Center or straight into a Studio project, letting you skip authoring the contract from scratch and jump straight to APIkit scaffolding. Because OAS is so broadly supported, this makes MuleSoft a practical implementation layer even for APIs whose specifications originate entirely outside the Anypoint ecosystem, which is one of the main reasons OAS adoption inside MuleSoft projects has grown steadily alongside RAML.

Key Points

  • OpenAPI is the industry-standard specification format, fully supported across Anypoint Platform.
  • OAS documents use paths and components/schemas with $ref for reuse.
  • APIkit routes and generates error flows identically whether the source spec is RAML or OAS.
  • The choice between RAML and OAS is largely organizational, not a technical limitation of Mule.

subtopics.title: API Scaffolding
subtopics.meta_description: Learn how APIkit scaffolding generates a complete, runnable Mule application skeleton directly from a RAML or OpenAPI specification in Studio or Maven.
subtopics.summary: How to generate a complete Mule flow skeleton from a RAML or OAS contract using APIkit scaffolding in Studio or Maven.
subtopics.content_html:
Hand-writing dozens of resource and method flows that mirror a RAML or OAS specification is tedious and error-prone. API scaffolding automates that first step: APIkit reads the specification and generates a complete, runnable Mule application skeleton — the router flow, one flow per resource/method combination, and the standard error-handling flows — in a single action.

Scaffolding in Anypoint Studio

After importing or creating a RAML/OAS file in your Mule project (typically under src/main/resources/api), right-clicking the file and choosing the APIkit scaffolding option generates:

  • An apikit:config element referencing the specification file.
  • A main flow containing an HTTP listener and the apikit:router.
  • One flow per resource/method pair, correctly named using the method:\resource:config convention.
  • Standard error flows (not found, method not allowed, bad request, etc.) wired to appropriate HTTP status codes.
<flow name="customer-api-main">
    <http:listener path="/api/*" config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" />
    <apikit:router config-ref="customer-api-config" />
    <error-handler ref="customer-api-apikitGlobalExceptionMapping" />
</flow>

<flow name="get:\customers:customer-api-config">
    <set-payload value='#[%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[]]' />
</flow>

Generated flows start with placeholder logic (an empty payload or a static example) so the application runs and returns valid responses immediately, before any real business logic has been written. Developers then replace the placeholder with a flow-ref to real implementation subflows.

Scaffolding From the Command Line / Maven

Scaffolding is also available through the APIkit Maven plugin, which is useful for automated project generation in CI pipelines or for regenerating flows as part of a build step when a specification changes:

# pom.xml excerpt
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.mule.tools.maven</groupId>
  <artifactId>mule-maven-plugin</artifactId>
</plugin>

Re-Scaffolding After Spec Changes

When the RAML/OAS contract changes — a new resource or method is added — re-running the scaffolding process adds the new flows needed to match the updated specification without touching flows that already exist. This lets the implementation stay in lockstep with an evolving contract with minimal manual rework, as long as developers followed the thin-router-flow pattern and kept custom logic in separately named subflows rather than editing the generated flows directly.

Recommended Workflow

  1. Finalize the RAML/OAS contract in Design Center and publish it to Exchange.
  2. Import the asset into a Mule project in Studio.
  3. Run APIkit scaffolding to generate the routing skeleton.
  4. Immediately replace generated placeholder logic with a single flow-ref per flow, delegating to a subflow.
  5. Implement business logic inside the subflows, leaving generated flows untouched for safe re-scaffolding later.
Tip: Never put business logic directly inside a generated resource/method flow. Keeping it as a thin flow-ref means future re-scaffolding never risks overwriting your implementation.

Key Points

  • Scaffolding auto-generates a runnable Mule skeleton directly from a RAML or OAS contract.
  • Generated flows are named by convention and include default error-handling flows.
  • Available both in Anypoint Studio's UI and through Maven for automated builds.
  • Delegate logic to subflows immediately so re-scaffolding stays safe after spec changes.

subtopics.title: API Versioning
subtopics.meta_description: Compare URI, header and query parameter versioning strategies for MuleSoft APIs, and see how API Manager manages a separate instance for every version.
subtopics.summary: An overview of API versioning strategies and how versions are managed across RAML/OAS contracts and API Manager instances.
subtopics.content_html:
APIs evolve. New fields get added, resources are restructured, and occasionally breaking changes are unavoidable. API versioning is the discipline of managing those changes so existing consumers keep working while new capabilities roll out, and MuleSoft supports several complementary versioning approaches across the specification, the implementation, and API Manager governance.

Versioning Strategies

StrategyExampleNotes
URI versioning/v1/customers, /v2/customersMost common and explicit; easy for consumers to see and pin a version.
Header versioningAccept: application/vnd.example.v2+jsonKeeps URIs stable; version negotiated through content negotiation.
Query parameter versioning/customers?version=2Simple but easy to omit accidentally; less common in production APIs.

Versioning in RAML/OAS

RAML has a native version property that is commonly interpolated directly into the baseUri, driving URI-based versioning automatically:

#%RAML 1.0
title: Customer API
version: v2
baseUri: https://api.example.com/{version}

OpenAPI does not have a dedicated version-in-URI mechanism built in, so URI versioning is typically expressed directly in the servers block, while the info.version field tracks the semantic version of the document itself (e.g. 1.4.0), which is more about document/change tracking than routing.

Versioning at the Implementation Level

A new major version is usually implemented as a separate APIkit configuration and its own set of generated flows, often within the same Mule application or as a distinct deployable artifact, depending on how independently the versions need to evolve and scale.

<http:listener path="/v1/api/*" config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" />
<apikit:router config-ref="customer-api-v1-config" />

<http:listener path="/v2/api/*" config-ref="HTTP_Listener_config" />
<apikit:router config-ref="customer-api-v2-config" />

Managing Versions in API Manager

Anypoint API Manager treats each version of an API as a distinct API instance, each with its own endpoint, applied policies, SLA tiers, and analytics. This lets you:

  • Apply different rate-limiting or security policies per version.
  • Track adoption and deprecate an older version only once traffic has migrated away from it.
  • Use API Manager's Autodiscovery, configured via a policy or the <api-gateway:autodiscovery> element (or the equivalent Anypoint Platform config in newer runtimes), to bind a running Mule application to a specific managed API instance so policies apply at runtime.

Semantic Versioning for Contracts

Beyond the URI version, it's good practice to apply semantic versioning (major.minor.patch) to the specification asset published in Exchange. Non-breaking additions (new optional fields, new endpoints) bump the minor or patch version without requiring consumers to change anything; breaking changes (removed fields, changed types, altered required behavior) demand a new major version and, typically, a new URI segment.

Tip: Favor additive, backward-compatible changes whenever possible — adding an optional field rarely justifies a new major version, while removing or renaming one almost always does.

Key Points

  • URI versioning is the most common and explicit strategy in MuleSoft APIs, often driven by RAML's version property.
  • Each API version is typically its own APIkit configuration and, in API Manager, its own API instance.
  • API Manager lets you apply distinct policies and monitor adoption per version.
  • Use semantic versioning on the contract itself to signal breaking vs non-breaking changes to consumers.
